questions.q: What three properties describe the blockchain in lesson 1?
a: Distributed, cryptographic and immutable
Centralized, encrypted and editable
Distributed, public and deletable
Private, temporary and centralized
questions.why: Lesson 1 names distributed, cryptographic and immutable as the blockchain's three main properties.

questions.q: What happens when a new Bitcoin transaction is recorded?
a: A new block is added, and the miner who adds it is paid in Bitcoin
A bank verifies the payment and charges a small fee
The transaction is deleted once the network confirms it
A government agency stores a copy in its own database
questions.why: Lesson 1 says miners compete to add each new block because doing so earns them Bitcoin.

questions.q: Which comparison does the author use for crypto's disruptive potential?
a: Email replacing snail mail and Netflix displacing Blockbuster
Radio replacing newspapers and television replacing radio
Cars replacing horses and planes replacing trains
Credit cards replacing cash and ATMs replacing bank tellers
questions.why: Lesson 2 compares Bitcoin's future impact to email overtaking mail and Netflix overtaking Blockbuster.

questions.q: What is the "speculation of crowds" the summary warns about?
a: Copying other investors without understanding what you are buying
Buying only assets that have already fallen sharply in price
Investing a fixed amount at the same time every month
Selling everything as soon as the market becomes popular
questions.why: Lesson 3 describes people piling into an asset simply because they see others doing it.

questions.q: How does the summary suggest reducing crypto risk?
a: Diversify, and track how your assets respond to world events
Put all your money into the single cheapest coin available
Follow the most confident voices on social media
Ignore economic news and never review your holdings
questions.why: Lesson 3 recommends diversifying and understanding how your asset reacts to economic conditions.
